input.contentScopeRationale: LAB-MATH-C (Festival Team Challenge) asks for independent transfer across facts, arrays, and multiplication word problems, but three of its eight items hinge on locating and solving for an unknown that is NOT the total: item 2 (40 flags in 5 equal rows -> group size unknown), item 3 (___ x 8 = 48 -> missing factor), and item 8 (36 lights split into equal-row arrays -> unknown row/column pairs). Confirmed unassisted graded work shows exactly this position is where the learner fails (missing_factor 0.3333 at evaluation:c8fdaacd3e1b0c13; equal_sharing 0 at evaluation:b81e075d2126c022), with the preregistered error - multiplying the two given numbers instead of solving for the missing group size - observed verbatim. Constructs that are already at 1.00 on graded work (equal_groups, arrays as computation, word_problem_interpretation at evaluation:a27f078c804e15e1 and evaluation:1b7d71227bc7fff2) are held as context and used only as contrast material, not re-taught. So the program teaches the underlying idea - in any equal-groups situation, groups x size = total, and which slot is empty determines whether you multiply or divide - rather than reproducing the eight worksheet questions. Numbers stay inside the assignment's fact range (products to 48-56, factors 3-9) so the work is comparable to the worksheet without copying it.

concept.name: Solving for the unknown position in an equal-groups relationship
concept.statement: Every equal-groups situation links three quantities: number of groups x size of each group = total. When the total is unknown you multiply the two known numbers; when the total is known and one factor is missing, you must find the number that multiplies to reach the total (divide or use a known fact), not multiply the two numbers you can see.
concept.instanceScope: LAB-MATH-C Festival Team Challenge, Grade 3. Applies to festival-style equal-groups contexts within products to 56 and factors 3-9: teams of children, flags in equal rows, cups per booth, tokens per bag, and equal-row arrays of stage lights. Covers missing-factor equations (___ x 8 = 48), equal-sharing group size (40 flags in 5 equal rows), and array row/column pairs for a known total (36 lights), with total-unknown items used only as contrast.

assumptions.claim: The learner's failures on LAB-MATH-B were a single scoped weakness in identifying and solving the unknown position, not a general multiplication deficit, and the same weakness will surface on LAB-MATH-C items 2, 3, and 8.
assumptions.uncertainty: The equal_sharing side rests on a single graded item (observation:d1b81984c24d6d80), and one missing-factor item was correct (observation:2aa76118c8657331) without a record of whether the number pairing was easier, so the width of the gap is not well estimated.

assumptions.claim: Multiplication computation, array reading, and equal-groups story interpretation are intact enough to serve as contrast anchors rather than instructional targets in this program.
assumptions.uncertainty: Each of these constructs rests on only two to three graded items from single same-day sources with exposure recorded as 'unknown', so prior familiarity with the exact items cannot be ruled out and durability over days is untested.

assumptions.claim: Requiring the learner to name which quantity is unknown before computing will reduce the multiply-the-given-numbers substitution more than additional undifferentiated practice would.
assumptions.uncertainty: This mechanism has never been tested with this child; the prior decision only recommended it. The learner may tag the unknown slot correctly and still multiply in the solve stage, which was itself preregistered as a possible error.

assumptions.claim: After instruction on the unknown position, some items where the total genuinely is unknown will be answered by dividing, because the learner over-applies the new rule.
assumptions.uncertainty: Purely predicted; no observation of over-correction exists for this child because no unknown-position instruction has yet been delivered.

assumptions.claim: The four recorded engagement events are activity-level facts only and cannot establish a durable format preference for this child.
assumptions.uncertainty: Each format appears exactly once, ratings are confounded with whatever academic content was inside, and the abandoned speed route may reflect pacing, difficulty, or novelty rather than dislike of the format.

input.academicTheory: The child can compute equal-groups products and read arrays reliably, and can interpret equal-groups stories, but treats every problem containing two visible numbers as a signal to multiply them. When the total is the number that is given and a factor is the number that is missing, the habit misfires: 40 flags in 5 rows becomes 200, and ___ x 8 = 48 becomes 384-style reasoning or a guess. The theory is therefore that the deficit is positional, not computational. If the learner is taught to map any equal-groups situation onto groups x size = total, mark which of the three slots is empty, and only then choose multiply (empty total) or find-the-factor (empty factor), unknown-position accuracy should rise into a realistic 0.55-0.85 band on unassisted practice, while total-unknown accuracy stays high but may dip slightly from over-correction. The array items are the strongest test of the theory because a total of 36 lights forces the learner to search factor pairs rather than multiply what is visible; success there would show the positional mapping generalized beyond a single sentence frame. This baseline is practice_only evidence: it can support or weaken the theory but cannot be treated as mastery, which requires confirmed unassisted graded work and a delayed reassessment.
